title: Untouched by pain and pleasure
hook: the one untouched by pleasure, pain, greed, attachment and pride is the Lord's image (Salok M9, ang 1427)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghatt, and your line: in every heart. Did you do one kindness for someone you'd usually pass by? The Lord lives in every vessel. Today's salok says what it looks like when that light shines through. Day five hundred ninety-three.

Watch someone near the bakery counter at the end of a long day. The smell hits. The craving arrives like a wave: just one, you deserve it, you've had a terrible afternoon. They stand there. And sometimes, if they simply wait, something surprising happens. The wave crests, and then it falls. Thirty seconds later, the want is smaller. Two minutes later, it's gone. From the inside, a craving can feel permanent. This one wasn't. The thirteenth salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur describes a person these waves can't knock over, and then gives that person a startling name.
screen: `THE BAKERY COUNTER.` → `A CRAVING, LIKE A WAVE.` → `IT CRESTS, THEN FALLS.`

segments.voice: The salok says, in paraphrase: the one whom pleasure and pain don't touch, nor greed, attachment or pride: says Nanak, listen, O mind, that one is the very image of God. The key verb is parsai, to touch, to brush against. These waves come to everyone. The salok doesn't say this person never meets pleasure or pain, greed or pride. It says they come and don't stick, like rain running down a window while the glass stays clear. Then the startling name: moorat bhagvaan, the image of God. Moorat means a form, an image, the word used for statues in temples. Sikhs don't worship images. And yet here, in the last pages of the Granth, the ninth Guru uses that very word for a living person. Not a statue, but someone free. To show God's image, the salok points not to stone but to a human being whose heart isn't pushed around. You might remember the Mool Mantar, the opening of the Granth, which calls God akaal moorat, the form beyond time. The same word, moorat. In the Mool Mantar it describes the Timeless. In this salok it describes a person who has become clear enough to show it. Notice how this builds on yesterday. The salok before this one said the Lord lives in every heart. In this picture, the waves of craving and pride cover that light, the way waves cover the sand. When they settle, it shows. So becoming untouched isn't about becoming hard. It's about becoming clear, so the One already inside can be seen.
screen: `PARSAI: THE WAVES DON'T STICK.` · `MOORAT BHAGVAAN: GOD'S IMAGE.` · `AKAAL MOORAT, THE SAME WORD.` · `CLEAR ENOUGH TO SHOW THE LIGHT.` · then, large: `UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one craving pass. Sit and breathe, and wait for any want to arise: to check your phone, to snack, to move, to stop sitting. When it comes, don't act and don't fight. Just watch it, like a wave. Feel where it sits in the body. Notice it rise, crest, and begin to fall. Count the breaths it takes. If another comes, watch that one too. You're practicing being touched without being moved. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Moorat, a form, an image. The thirteenth salok calls the one whom pleasure, pain, greed, attachment and pride don't touch moorat bhagvaan, the very image of God.
Your line: untouched. Today, when a craving comes, wait three breaths before you act. Just three. Watch the wave, and see what's left. Day five hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok among the ninth Guru's saloks at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and often cite it to say that a person free of craving and pride shows the image of God.

original.note: Gurmukhi: moorat, form or image. The Mool Mantar says akaal moorat; this salok says moorat bhagvaan.

trapdoor: what you thought: untouched means cold, feeling nothing.
what it means: the waves of pleasure, pain and craving come, but don't stick, so the light within can show.
what a scholar hears: in a tradition that rejects image worship, the ninth Guru uses moorat, the word for a temple image, for a free human being, echoing the Mool Mantar's akaal moorat.
